name: Walking Lunge
tierNote: Safety tier B from content.md appendix B (loaded lunges and split squats); census.json difficulty tier 2.

inherit.why: true for this child because it is also a front-to-back split stance in the sagittal plane, so shin angle, trunk and back-knee depth all read from the side.
true for this child because the front knee bends under body weight or load exactly as in the reverse lunge; the NHS knee box is re-cited in this card.
true for this child because its own technique source lists dumbbells held at the sides, the parent's drawn hold; the claim is re-cited in this card.

claims.text: In the walking lunge the back foot steps forward to meet and pass the front foot after each rep, instead of the front foot stepping back.

quotes.text: It can also be done as a walking lunge—rather than stepping back with the front foot after each rep, step the back foot forward to meet the front foot.

claims.text: Each step: step forward and bend both knees until the back knee very lightly touches the floor, with a step long enough that the front shin is about vertical.

quotes.text: Starting in your squat stance, step one leg forward and bend both knees until the back knee very lightly touches the floor.
Step long enough that in this bottom position, the front shin is approximately vertical.

claims.text: On landing, lower the hips toward the floor rather than driving them forward (aim the back knee toward the front heel); this limits how far the shin travels forward. Source is ACE's walking lunge with a medicine-ball twist, so the twist does not apply.

quotes.text: As you lunge forward, focus more on lowering your hips towards the floor rather than driving your hips forward, (think about aiming your left knee towards the heel of your right foot).
This will help control the amount of forward movement of your shinbone (forward tibial translation) over your foot.

claims.text: To move on, push the front foot into the floor to stand, then lift the back leg and swing it forward into the next lunge (ACE walking lunge with twist; the twist does not apply).

quotes.text: firmly push the right foot in to the ground and pull yourself back to a standing position
pick the left leg off of the ground and slowly swing it forward to initiate the next lunge.

claims.text: The stepping foot lands heel first and the weight moves onto it slowly, without the upper body tilting sideways (ACE walking lunge with twist; the twist does not apply).

quotes.text: The right (swing) leg should initiate contact with a heel strike first, slowly transferring your body weight into the right (leading / forward) foot placed firmly on the floor.
avoid any sideways tilting or swaying in your upper body

claims.text: Start standing with the feet about hip width apart.

quotes.text: Starting Position: Stand with your feet about hip width apart.

claims.text: Loading a lunge too heavily costs the controlled descent, the upright trunk and the balance between the feet; if any of these is lost, reduce the weight.

quotes.text: Many athletes try to load lunges too heavily and lose the position in which the exercise will be most effective.
If you can’t maintain a controlled descent into the bottom of the lunge, maintain an upright trunk, and maintain balance between the feet, reduce the weight.

claims.text: Lunge programming: loaded sets of 3-10 reps per leg at a weight that keeps a full-length step and smooth movement with no crash into the bottom; light or unloaded lunges can be done for 15-20 reps.

quotes.text: Sets of 3-10 reps per leg are usually appropriate with weight that allows a full length step, smooth movement and no crashing into the bottom position.
Light or unloaded lunges can be done with 15-20 reps as well if using them for work capacity or rehab.

claims.text: In an EMG study of static, step-forward and walking lunges (30 % body-weight load), a forward-inclined trunk about doubled lower-back (erector spinae) activity compared with a straight trunk. Walking lunges were one of the three tested.

quotes.text: Results indicate that positioning the trunk in a forward-inclined position induces greater lower lumbar erector spinae activation
(straight = 20 ± 15, inclined = 40 ± 29)

claims.text: In the same study the walking lunge produced more glute max and more lower-back activity than the static lunge.

quotes.text: (static = 24 ± 16, forward = 26 ± 22, walking = 40 ± 33)
(static = 31 ± 12, forward = 54 ± 20, walking = 58 ± 30)

claims.text: In a slow-lowering walking lunge, a longer-than-normal step did not raise thigh or hip muscle activity while lowering; it only made coming up harder, so a normal step length was judged enough.

quotes.text: Contrary to hypothesis, longer step lengths did not increase eccentric phase knee and hip extensor activities, but made the returning concentric phase movements more difficult.
Thus, a normal step length appears sufficient for ELW.

claims.text: A lunge can be loaded with dumbbells or kettlebells held at the sides, or with a barbell.

quotes.text: The lunge can be loaded in many ways, such as with a barbell in the clean rack position or overhead, dumbbells or kettlebells at the sides

claims.text: Step length shifts the emphasis: longer steps work the glutes and hamstrings more, shorter steps with the knee ahead of the toes work the quads more.

quotes.text: longer steps will emphasize the glutes and hamstrings more, and shorter steps with the knee moving in front of the toes will emphasize the quads more.

claims.text: In a loaded forward lunge with a stride, the quads and glutes were highly active and the hamstrings and calf (gastrocnemius) moderately active; this is a forward lunge study, applied to the walking lunge by analogy.

quotes.text: During the externally loaded forward lunge, high to very high muscle activity occurs in the quadriceps, gluteus maximus, and gluteus medius
while moderate muscle activity occurs in the hamstrings, gastrocnemius, and adductor longus.

claims.text: NHS knee-pain advice: get urgent advice (111) if the knee is very painful, or locks or gives way.

quotes.text: Get advice from 111 now if:
your knee is very painful
your knee locks, gives way or painfully clicks – painless clicking is normal

plate.viewWhy: Locomotion forward in the sagittal plane; the plate shows one step (census note). Shin angle (c2), hip drop (c3) and trunk (c7, c9) read from the side.
plate.equipment: Two dumbbells hanging at the sides (c12), floor line.
plate.start: Standing tall, feet about hip width apart (c6), dumbbells at the sides (c12).
plate.end: One foot stepped forward, back knee very lightly touching the floor, front shin about vertical (c2), trunk upright (c7).

checkpoints.label: Front shin vertical
checkpoints.what: At the bottom the front shin is about vertical.

checkpoints.label: Hips drop down
checkpoints.what: Hips lower toward the floor instead of driving forward.

checkpoints.label: Chest up
checkpoints.what: Trunk stays upright through the step.

mistake.what: Trunk pitches forward over the front thigh at the bottom (upright trunk lost).
mistake.why: The lunge anchor names it as a position lost to heavy loading (c7); a forward-inclined trunk doubled lower-back activity in a study that included walking lunges (c9), and the walking lunge already showed the most lower-back activity (c10).
mistake.rankNote: No source ranks walking-lunge faults by frequency. Sideways tilt (c5) needs a front view.

tells.text: Back knee lightly touches the floor

tempo.text: Controlled descent with a full-length step; no crash into the bottom. No source gives seconds for the standard walking lunge.

plate.variantLine: exercises.json lists Dumbbells / Barbell. The plate draws dumbbells at the sides (c12). Step, shin and trunk claims (c1, c2, c7) come from Catalyst's load-agnostic lunge page, so they hold for both.

grip.note: Thumb and wrist come from the shared hold archetype.

setup.step: Stand with feet about hip width apart, dumbbells at your sides.
Step forward, landing heel first, and let the weight move onto that foot slowly.
Drop the hips until the back knee lightly touches the floor, front shin about vertical.
Push the front foot into the floor to stand, then swing the back leg forward into the next step.
Keep alternating legs as you move forward.

posture.point: Front shin about vertical at the bottom.
A normal step length is enough.

handlingMistakes.mistake: Chest pitching forward at the bottom.
handlingMistakes.fix: Go lighter until you can stay upright and controlled.

handlingMistakes.mistake: Driving the hips and knee forward on landing.
handlingMistakes.fix: Drop the hips down; aim the back knee at the front heel.
Lower slowly; use a weight that lets you move smoothly.

rows.where: Front of the thigh and the glutes

rows.means: Usually means the chest is leaning forward.
rows.fix: Stay upright; go lighter if you can't.

rows.where: Knee pain that is very bad, or the knee locks or gives way

risks.risk: Too heavy a load costs the upright trunk, the controlled descent and balance.
Crashing into the bottom position instead of lowering under control.

zooms.right: Trunk upright over the hips at the bottom.
zooms.wrong: Chest pitched forward over the front thigh.

zooms.right: Hips dropped, front shin about vertical.
zooms.wrong: Hips driven forward, front shin tipped far forward.

libraryDiff.why: Library: quads and glutes primary, hamstrings and calves secondary, core stabilizer. Walking-lunge EMG (c10) supports glutes; forward-lunge EMG applied by analogy (c14) supports quads primary and hamstrings and calves secondary. No change.

loadProgression.text: Start light or unloaded; add weight only while the step stays full and the descent smooth.

anchorNote: Catalyst Athletics Lunge page read in full; it covers the walking lunge as a named variation (c1). ACE Walking Lunges with Twists page also read in full; its twist-specific steps are not used.
